opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we get a lot, and honestly I think it's one of the decisions I'm most comfortable with in hindsight.

When you start a new generation of models, there's always a temptation to change everything: new architecture, new attention variant, maybe mixture of experts, all the fancy stuff people are publishing. But the reality is that at the scale we operate, every change you introduce is a risk. Each one interacts with the others, and if something goes wrong in a run that costs that much compute, it's very hard to disentangle what caused it. So our philosophy was: what are the levers that actually matter most, and let's push those as far as we can.

And for us the answer was pretty clearly data and scale, more than architecture. The transformer as it is, with a few well-understood tweaks, is already very good. What changed dramatically between Llama 2 and Llama 3 was the amount and the quality of the data. We went to around fifteen trillion tokens, we put a lot of effort into filtering, deduplication, and the data mix, including much more code and multilingual data, and we trained well beyond what people would have called "compute-optimal." It turns out the models keep improving when you keep feeding them good tokens, and that matters a lot for inference, because you want the best model at a given size, not just the best model for a given training budget.

We did make some targeted changes. We moved to a bigger tokenizer, around 128K vocabulary, which helps compression and multilinguality. We used grouped-query attention across the sizes to make inference more efficient, and we extended the context length. But these are incremental, well-validated choices, not a reinvention.

There's also an organizational point. If you keep the architecture stable, the team can focus its energy on the things that move the needle: data, post-training, evaluation, scaling the infrastructure. Post-training in particular was a huge part of Llama 3: better preference data, iterating on rejection sampling and DPO-style methods, a lot of human annotation. That's where a lot of the gains in actual usefulness came from.

So I'd say it wasn't a lack of ambition. It was a bet that simplicity scales. I'm not saying architecture research doesn't matter; it will, and we'll explore things. But you should change the architecture when you have strong evidence it beats the baseline at scale, not because it's new. Most ideas that look great at small scale just don't hold up when you go big.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling data and training beyond compute-optimal, but does not identify allocating the same compute to every token as an architectural limitation.

r002.rationale: It says Llama 3’s changes centered more on data and scale than architecture, highlighting the increased amount and quality of training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we deliberately didn't try to be clever on architecture. If you look at Llama 3, it's still a dense transformer, still the standard decoder-only setup, basically the same recipe as Llama 2. The big changes were things like a much larger vocabulary, grouped query attention across all the sizes, longer context. But fundamentally it's the same object.

And the reason is that when you're training at that scale, every architectural change you make is a risk. You might get a few percent of efficiency, but you also might find out at two trillion tokens that something you did breaks in a way you didn't anticipate in the small-scale ablations. And you can't afford to restart. So the question we kept asking ourselves was, where does the improvement actually come from? And for us, the answer was pretty clearly data and scale. Fifteen trillion tokens versus two trillion, much better filtering, much more careful mixing of the data, a lot more code and multilingual. That's where the gains were. The architecture wasn't the bottleneck.

There's also a sort of philosophical point. A lot of the field, especially in academia, is incentivized to publish new architectures, because that's what gets you a paper. But if you're actually trying to ship the best model, novelty is not the goal. You want the thing that's robust, that scales predictably, that your whole infrastructure stack already knows how to run. Mixture of experts is a good example. It's interesting, it's probably where things go eventually, but it adds a lot of complexity in training and in serving, and at the time we weren't convinced it was worth it for what we were trying to do.

So I'd frame it as, we spent our risk budget on the places where we had evidence it would pay off. Data quality, scaling laws to pick the right sizes, and the post-training, which is where a huge amount of the work actually went. And keeping the architecture boring is what let us do that with confidence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses architectural risk and complexity, but does not identify equal compute per token as a limitation of current architectures.

r002.rationale: It says the gains came from data and scale, citing more tokens, better filtering, and careful data mixing, while describing architecture as not the bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of value in keeping things simple when you’re scaling. If you change the architecture, the data, and the training recipe all at once, it becomes very difficult to understand where the improvements are coming from—or what went wrong.

So keeping the architecture relatively similar doesn’t mean there’s no innovation. You can put a lot of the effort into the data, the quality of the training, and the post-training. And having a foundation that you understand lets you take those steps with more confidence. The question isn’t whether the architecture looks new; it’s whether the resulting model is better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses keeping architecture simple but does not identify equal compute per token as a limitation of current architectures.

r002.rationale: It says effort can go into data, training quality, and post-training, but does not identify training data as the principal focus of Llama 3’s changes relative to architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
The goal was to keep things relatively simple. If you change the architecture, the data, and the training recipe all at once, it becomes difficult to understand where the improvements come from. Keeping a fairly similar architecture gave us a stable foundation to focus on data quality, scale, and getting the training right.

That doesn’t mean there’s no room for architectural innovation. But you don’t need to change everything to make substantial progress. Sometimes the most valuable work is executing really well on a recipe that you already understand.
